title: Justice

segments.voice: Yesterday, prudence: practical wisdom, the right thing, the right way, the right time. Your line was wise in the moment. Did you stop to ask whether it was the time? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.

Rent. A phone bill. A borrowed book still on your shelf. A friend who covered lunch last time. A teacher, years back, who believed in you before anyone else did and never heard you say so. Make a list of what you owe and it gets long fast, and only some of it is money. Christian teachers took up an old, plain definition of justice: giving each their due. Not revenge, not a courtroom drama. Just the steady work of making sure everyone gets what is theirs. Today, the next cardinal virtue. Justice.

Paul comes close to that definition in his letter to the Romans: "Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour." Look at that list. Taxes and fees, yes. But also respect, and honor. Some debts are paid in money and some are paid in thanks, and Paul counts both. Proverbs adds the timing: "Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it." If you can pay it now, the delay itself is a small injustice. Then the prophets widen the frame from my bills to a whole society. Micah asks what the Lord requires, and the first answer is "to do justly." In Hebrew, that's to do mishpat, justice. Amos pictures it as something that should never dry up: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." A river, not a single payment. Justice keeps flowing toward whoever is owed, especially the people easiest to overlook. And then Paul says one more thing, right after the list of dues: "Owe no man any thing, but to love one another." Pay every debt you can, he says, except one. The debt of love stays open. You never get to mark it paid and walk away. Justice gives each their due. Love keeps on owing.

Here's the practice: find what you owe. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind walk slowly through your people and your week. A bill you've been putting off. Something borrowed. Someone owed an apology. Someone owed a thank-you they've never heard. Don't make a long list. Choose one debt, in money or in thanks, that it's in the power of your hand to pay today. Hold it clearly. If you pray, you can ask for help to pay it. The bell holds the time.
Justice. Giving each their due, in money, in honor, in thanks. In the Hebrew of the prophets, mishpat.
Your line: each their due. Today, pay the one debt you chose: the bill, the book, or the thank-you, said out loud or written down. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Christian moral teaching names justice among the cardinal virtues; churches teach it through paying fair debts and wages, giving thanks and respect, and working for the poor and overlooked, drawing on Micah 6:8 and the prophets.

original.note: Hebrew: justice, judgment; Micah's 'to do justly' is to do mishpat.

trapdoor: what you thought: justice means punishment.
what it means: giving each their due, in money and in thanks, and keeping it flowing like a river.
what a scholar hears: where the King James says judgment in Amos 5:24, the Hebrew is mishpat, the same word as Micah's 'do justly'.

notes: 'An old, plain definition of justice: giving each their due' (suum cuique; Justinian's Digest, taken up by Ambrose and Aquinas) is attributed to 'Christian teachers' without date or source; confirm.
'Paul writes the definition almost word for word' is an interpretive bridge from Romans 13:7; confirm it doesn't overstate.
Micah 6:8 עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט and Amos 5:24 מִשְׁפָּט: confirm the trapdoor and original note.

Editor pass: 'Paul writes the definition almost word for word' overstated Romans 13:7, now 'comes close to that definition'; screen line 'let justice run down as waters' corrected to the KJV's 'judgment'.
